In the second, it again changes to be longer, as they considered all the parts to be one larger whole split into 6 pieces. Furthermore, the pieces of the whole are not equal. In fraction models, the areas of the pieces of the whole must also all be equal.
data.thinking: The student may have been thinking that with fractions, we can always combine the numerator pieces, and count our numerator pieces over our total number of pieces. They may not have a robust understanding of how the parts of the whole must always be equal sizes.
data.feedback: When working with area models, beware that how big a part of the picture is is very important. Equal values should have equal area. Since the 2 is two wholes, and each whole is 4/4, we need to draw each of those left two boxes as rectangles just like your 3/4. Doing so will show us that we have 4 + 4 + 3 = 11 shaded pieces. Since each of the pieces is a fourth, we know 2 3/4 = 11/4. It is probably helpful to just keep the space in between the wholes, so we don't accidentally interpret the picture as meaning one whole giant whole with more than 4 parts.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to subtract
data.incorrect: The student subtracted incorrectly in the ones column and the hundreds column. Additionally, they regrouped from the thousands directly to make 10 more groups of ten, which is not allowed.
data.thinking: When subtracting 0 - 4 or 0 - 7, the student may have been thinking of 4 - 0 and 7 - 0. They may have also thought that the zero in the hundreds column has no value, and can be skipped over to directly give regrouped values to the tens column.
data.feedback: Be careful with the order of subtraction! If we have 0-4, we don't have enough ones in the minuend to subtract, and must regroup from the tens first. When regrouping over a zero, we cannot just skip it. Bring the regrouped 1 from the thousands place over to the hundreds column. One group of one thousand is ten groups of one hundred. Now we can split apart those hundreds, take one away to leave us with 9 in the hundreds column, and give it as a ten (floating 1) in the tens column.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to multiply
data.incorrect: The student added 4 + 6 instead of multiplying. They also seemed unsure of what to do with the 11 in the second chute, and simply smushed it together with the surrounding digits in the final product.
data.thinking: Since they multiplied every other partial product correctly, the student probably just lost track of what operation they were performing with 4 and 6. The student may not remember that this algorithm sometimes requires that we regroup after the adding step.
data.feedback: Be careful, 4 times 6 shoul be 24, not 10. After adding diagonally, check that we only have one digit at the end of each chute. If not, we need to regroup. Your 11 needs to have its first digit regrouped to the next chute. Like the standard algorithm, you could place this above the chute. Or, you could place it at the bottom. Either way, we need to add 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 to get 6 in the hundreds chute.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to add
data.incorrect: Each time they went to regroup to the next column, the student placed the ones instead of the tens. For instance, in 6 + 7 = 13, they placed the 3 above the tens column, instead of the 1.
data.thinking: This student may not have an understanding of why we regroup. They may have been thinking that one of the two digits needs to be placed above the next column, but not have an understanding of why this is so.
data.feedback: You've got the idea of the algorithm, but we need to be careful which number we are regrouping to the next column each time. For instance, with 6 + 7 = 13, the 13 represents 1 group of ten and 3 ones left over. That means the 3 is what needs to stay in our ones column, and the 1 is what needs to move over to the tens column. Each time we regroup a number, its left (higher place value) digit will be moved above the next column to the left (the next higher place value).

Finally, be sure that all your final values in each column are less than ten, and all regrouping is done, before writing your final answer.

data.thinking: They may have learned or invented a shortcut for turning division of fractions into multiplication. Or, they may have conflated the process with cross multiplication. They also may have thought that any operations (such as subtraction) are permitted when simplifying fractions, instead of only multiplication or division.
data.feedback: Remember that when we think of fraction division as you were here, we are thinking of multiplying the first fraction by the second fraction's reciprocal. I would encourage you to write out the extra step where we change the problem to 4/3 times 5/2, then multiply across horizontally as usual. Also, we can't subtract equal amounts from numerator and denominator and obtain an equivalent fraction. We can only multiply or divide both by the same amount. Consider if we were to do the same subtracting of 1 and 1 to the fraction 2/3. We would get 1/2, which is much smaller than 2/3.

data.incorrect: The student subtracted incorrectly in the ones column and the hundreds column. Additionally, they regrouped from the thousands directly to make 10 more groups of ten, which is not allowed.
data.thinking: When subtracting 0 - 4 or 0 - 7, the student may have been thinking of 4 - 0 and 7 - 0. They may have also thought that the zero in the hundreds column has no value, and can be skipped over to directly give regrouped values to the tens column.
data.feedback: Be careful with the order of subtraction! If we have 0-4, we don't have enough ones in the minuend to subtract, and must regroup from the tens first. When regrouping over a zero, we cannot just skip it. Bring the regrouped 1 from the thousands place over to the hundreds column. One group of one thousand is ten groups of one hundred. Now we can split apart those hundreds, take one away to leave us with 9 in the hundreds column, and give it as a ten (floating 1) in the tens column.

data.feedback: You did a good job adding each place value's digits together. What this does for us is align the regrouped values and non-regrouped values diagonally, so that every pair of numbers in a diagonal chute belongs to the same place value. Add diagonally in this algorithm, along the chutes.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to divide
data.incorrect: The student did not move the decimal on both dividend and divisor far enough. They should move the decimal at least two places, so that the divisor is a whole number. The student also did not continue dividing until they arrived at zero or found a repeating decimal pattern. Instead, they treated the 10 as a sort of remainder after the decimal point.
data.thinking: The student may have been thinking that we only need to move the decimals until the dividend is a whole number. They may have also thought that remainders and amounts after the decimal point are interchangable.
data.feedback: Make sure to move the decimals on both numbers until the divisor is a whole number, not the dividend. Moving the decimal is actually just multiplying both numbers by 10, so there is no harm in continuing past the last digit of the dividend. We can place an extra zero at the end of the dividend. If we are dividing with decimal numbers, we don't usually have a concept of remainder. We need to bring down the next digits one at a time (all zeros from here on out) and continue the long division process until it stops or we find a repeating pattern.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to divide
data.incorrect: The student did not move the decimal on both dividend and divisor far enough. They should move the decimal at least two places, so that the divisor is a whole number. The student also did not continue dividing until they arrived at zero or found a repeating decimal pattern. Instead, they treated the 10 as a sort of remainder after the decimal point.
data.thinking: The student may have been thinking that we only need to move the decimals until the dividend is a whole number. They may have also thought that remainders and amounts after the decimal point are interchangable.
data.feedback: Make sure to move the decimals on both numbers until the divisor is a whole number, not the dividend. Moving the decimal is actually just multiplying both numbers by 10, so there is no harm in continuing past the last digit of the dividend. We can place an extra zero at the end of the dividend. If we are dividing with decimal numbers, we don't usually have a concept of remainder. We need to bring down the next digits one at a time (all zeros from here on out) and continue the long division process until it stops or we find a repeating pattern.

data.incorrect: First, the student did not align the digits of the quotient with the correct digits of the dividend. Since 15 does not divide 6, we move over to include the 3 to look at 63. The first digit of the quotient should be placed above the 3. Next, the student underestimated how many 15s are in 63, and said 3 instead of 4. Finally, the student tried to multiply 12 times 15 to account for how many times 15 goes into 182. However, we should not use more than one digit at a time in the quotients in the standard algorithm.
data.thinking: The student probably didn't realize that the partial remainder of 18 is larger than 15, or that such a result means we've made a mistake in the standard algorithm. They may also not have realized that the placement of the digits in the quotient hold meaning.
data.feedback: Always be careful where you place your digits in your quotient. Each should be placed above the rightmost digit of the number we are currently subtracting from. Also be careful to check partial remainders before bringing down another dividend digit. In your case, 18 is greater than 15, which means we need to go back, erase the 3, and figure out what higher amount of 15s can fit in 63.

data.work_desc_1: The student was trying to subtract
data.incorrect: The student subtracted incorrectly in the ones column and the hundreds column. Additionally, they regrouped from the thousands directly to make 10 more groups of ten, which is not allowed.
data.thinking: When subtracting 0 - 4 or 0 - 7, the student may have been thinking of 4 - 0 and 7 - 0. They may have also thought that the zero in the hundreds column has no value, and can be skipped over to directly give regrouped values to the tens column.
data.feedback: Be careful with the order of subtraction! If we have 0-4, we don't have enough ones in the minuend to subtract, and must regroup from the tens first. When regrouping over a zero, we cannot just skip it. Bring the regrouped 1 from the thousands place over to the hundreds column. One group of one thousand is ten groups of one hundred. Now we can split apart those hundreds, take one away to leave us with 9 in the hundreds column, and give it as a ten (floating 1) in the tens column.

data.feedback: Make sure to move the decimals on both numbers until the divisor is a whole number, not the dividend. Moving the decimal is actually just multiplying both numbers by 10, so there is no harm in continuing past the last digit of the dividend. We can place an extra zero at the end of the dividend. If we are dividing with decimal numbers, we don't usually have a concept of remainder. We need to bring down the next digits one at a time (all zeros from here on out) and continue the long division process until it stops or we find a repeating pattern.

data.problem: Jayla's family has 38 hens. Each hen lays 2 eggs per day. They collect eggs for 3 days and pack them in cartons of 12 eggs. If each dozen can be sold for <m>\$4</m>, how many full dozens can they sell, how many eggs will be left over, and how much money will they make from selling the full dozens?
data.solution: Total eggs: <m>38 \times 2 \times 3 = 228</m> eggs. Packing them into cartons of 12: <m>228 \div 12 = 19</m> exactly, with no eggs left over. Only the 19 full dozens can be sold: <m>19 \times \$4 = \$76</m>.

data.problem: One fall night, the temperature rose 9 degrees between 1:00 AM and 3:00 AM. By 8:00 AM, the temperature tripled from what it was at 3:00 AM. By 1:00 PM, it rose 6 degrees from what it was at 8:00 AM. If the temperature was <m>24</m> degrees at 1:00 PM, what was the original temperature at 1:00 AM?
data.solution: The final temperature is given and the starting one is not, so work backwards, undoing each change in turn. At 1:00 PM it was <m>24</m> degrees. Between 8:00 AM and 1:00 PM the temperature rose 6 degrees, so take them away: <m>24 - 6 = 18</m>, so at 8:00 AM it was <m>18</m> degrees. Between 3:00 AM and 8:00 AM the temperature tripled, so divide: <m>18 \div 3 = 6</m>, so at 3:00 AM it was <m>6</m> degrees. Between 1:00 AM and 3:00 AM the temperature rose 9 degrees, so take those away: <m>6 - 9 = -3</m>. The original temperature was <m>-3</m> degrees.

data.problem: Hunter's mom is trying to find a contractor to work on their house. The first contractor charges <m>\$52</m> per hour. The second contractor charges <m>\$67</m> per hour, but Hunter's mom found a special deal online which will deduct <m>\$228</m> from the total bill. If his mom needs the chosen contractor to work for 13 hours, how will the potential bills compare? Which contractor is the better deal?
data.solution: To find the total cost for each contractor, we multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours needed. The total cost for the first contractor is <m>\$52</m> per hour multiplied by 13 hours, which equals <m>\$676</m>. The total cost for the second contractor is <m>\$67</m> per hour multiplied by 13 hours minus the <m>\$228</m> discount, which equals <m>\$643</m>. Therefore, the total bill will be <m>\$33</m> more if they choose the first contractor. Hunter and his mom should hire the second contractor.

data.problem: Bailey's family is buying a new house. The agreed-upon price for the house at the time of closing is <m>\$271{,}333</m>. The bank requires an immediate down payment of <m>\$24{,}273</m>. The remaining amount will be paid over 227 equal monthly payments, plus one more month for any remaining balance. Assuming there is no interest involved, how much will Bailey's family be paying each month? Don't forget to mention the final month, in case there was a remaining balance.
data.solution: To find out how much Bailey's family will need to pay each month, we first subtract the down payment from the house price to find the remaining amount. <m>\$271{,}333</m> minus <m>\$24{,}273</m> equals <m>\$247{,}060</m>. Dividing this by 227 monthly payments, we get <m>\$1{,}088</m> per month. Therefore, Bailey's family will need to pay <m>\$1{,}088</m> each month for 227 months, followed by a final payment of <m>\$84</m>.

data.problem: Mateo is ordering pizza for a party of 20 people. Each person will eat 2 slices. Each pizza has 6 slices and costs <m>\$18</m>. What is the fewest number of whole pizzas Mateo should order to have enough slices for everyone, and how much will the order cost?
data.solution: Total slices needed: <m>20 \times 2 = 40</m> slices. Each pizza has 6 slices, so divide the slices among whole pizzas: <m>40 \div 6 = 6</m> with 4 slices left over, and those still need one more, so 7 pizzas. Total cost: <m>7 \times \$18 = \$126</m>.

data.problem: Claire is walking down a straight road from her house to the market. She walks 1/2 mi. before taking a rest. Then, she keeps walking another 1 1/4 mi. At that point, she realizes that she already walked past the market, and backtracks 1/2 mi. to get to the market. How far is it from Claire's house to the market?
data.solution: To find out the total distance from Claire's house to the market, we add the distances she walked and then subtract the distance she backtracked. 1/2 mi. plus 1 1/4 mi. equals 1 3/4 mi. Then, subtracting the 1/2 mi. backtracked, we get 1 1/4 mi. Therefore, the total distance from Claire's house to the market is 1 1/4 mi.

data.problem: Evelyn has a lemonade recipe that makes 10 cups using 5 scoops of sugar and 6 lemons. Evelyn expects 31 customers and plans for each customer to have 2 cup(s). How many full recipes does she need to make to have enough lemonade, how much sugar and how many lemons are needed in total, and does she have enough supplies if 33 scoops of sugar and 40 lemons are on hand? Show the computations and explain any shortages or extras.
data.solution: Cups needed: <m>31 \times 2 = 62</m> cups. One recipe makes 10 cups, so <m>62 \div 10 = 6</m> with 2 cups left over, and those still need one more, so 7 recipes. Sugar needed: <m>7 \times 5 = 35</m> scoops. Lemons needed: <m>7 \times 6 = 42</m> lemons. On hand: 33 scoops sugar, 40 lemons. Sugar status: short of sugar by 2 scoop(s). Lemon status: short of lemons by 2 lemon(s).

data.problem: Taylor's mom is trying to find a contractor to work on their house. The first contractor charges <m>\$53</m> per hour. The second contractor charges <m>\$71</m> per hour, but Taylor's mom found a special deal online which will deduct <m>\$297</m> from the total bill. If her mom needs the chosen contractor to work for 14 hours, how will the potential bills compare? Which contractor is the better deal?
data.solution: To find the total cost for each contractor, we multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours needed. The total cost for the first contractor is <m>\$53</m> per hour multiplied by 14 hours, which equals <m>\$742</m>. The total cost for the second contractor is <m>\$71</m> per hour multiplied by 14 hours minus the <m>\$297</m> discount, which equals <m>\$697</m>. Therefore, the total bill will be <m>\$45</m> more if they choose the first contractor. Taylor and her mom should hire the second contractor.

data.problem: One winter night, the temperature rose 4 degrees between 2:00 AM and 9:00 AM. By 11:00 AM, the temperature tripled from what it was at 9:00 AM. By 3:00 PM, it fell 11 degrees from what it was at 11:00 AM. If the temperature was <m>-2</m> degrees at 3:00 PM, what was the original temperature at 2:00 AM?
data.solution: The final temperature is given and the starting one is not, so work backwards, undoing each change in turn. At 3:00 PM it was <m>-2</m> degrees. Between 11:00 AM and 3:00 PM the temperature fell 11 degrees, so add them back: <m>-2 + 11 = 9</m>, so at 11:00 AM it was <m>9</m> degrees. Between 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM the temperature tripled, so divide: <m>9 \div 3 = 3</m>, so at 9:00 AM it was <m>3</m> degrees. Between 2:00 AM and 9:00 AM the temperature rose 4 degrees, so take those away: <m>3 - 4 = -1</m>. The original temperature was <m>-1</m> degrees.

data.problem: Declan is making some Christmas decorations with twine, but he is running out of twine to use! He measures his remaining twine before starting his projects. Will Declan have enough twine to make all three projects? Why or why not?
data.solution: To find out if Declan has enough twine to complete all three projects, we first calculate the total amount of twine available. Adding the two spools gives us 1 ft + 2 3/5 ft, which equals 3 3/5 ft of twine. Then, we add up the amount of twine needed for each project. Summing up 1/2 ft + 1 1/2 ft + 1 3/4 ft gives us a total of 3 3/4 ft of twine needed overall. Declan does not have enough twine to complete all three projects because he needs 3 3/4 ft and has 3 3/5 ft on hand.

data.problem: Julian's family is traveling to their cottage for vacation. Yesterday, they drove from 10:00 AM to 7:00 PM, with no stops until they made it to their hotel for the night. In that time, they drove 450 miles. Today Julian's family continued driving at the same average speed for eight more hours, after which they arrived at the cottage. During the past two days, how many miles did they travel to get to their cottage?
data.solution: First, we must determine their average speed. That is, we want to find how many miles they travel for each hour of driving. Dividing the first day's distance of 450 miles by 9 hours gives us 50 mph. Now we can calculate the number of miles driven on the second day by multiplying 50 mph by 8 hours, yielding 400 miles. Finally, adding together both distances gives a total of 850 miles.

data.problem: Lauren's family has 15 hens. Each hen lays 1 eggs per day. They collect eggs for 4 days and pack them in cartons of 12 eggs. If each dozen can be sold for <m>\$3</m>, how many full dozens can they sell, how many eggs will be left over, and how much money will they make from selling the full dozens?
data.solution: Total eggs: <m>15 \times 1 \times 4 = 60</m> eggs. Packing them into cartons of 12: <m>60 \div 12 = 5</m> exactly, with no eggs left over. Only the 5 full dozens can be sold: <m>5 \times \$3 = \$15</m>.

data.problem: Jordyn runs a small cookie stand every weekend. This weekend, she started by baking 18 trays of cookies. Each tray fits 13 cookies at a time. On Friday, she sold 214 cookies. So, she decided to make 3 more trays of cookies on Saturday morning. She then sold 36 cookies on Saturday, and 17 cookies on Sunday. She will bring the extra remaining cookies to school to share with her class on Monday. How many cookies does she have to share with her class?
data.solution: To find out how many cookies Jordyn has to share with her class, we could first calculate the total number of cookies baked. So, 18 trays multiplied by 13 cookies per tray equals 234 cookies. After that, she baked 3 more trays of cookies, which adds another 39 cookies. The total number of cookies baked throughout the weekend was 273. Adding together the cookies sold on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, gives a total of  267 cookies. Subtracting this from the total 273 cookies cooked, there are 6 cookies left. Therefore, Jordyn has 6 cookies to share with her class.

data.problem: Eden is packing 6 shelves of books with 27 books on each shelf into moving boxes. Each box holds 11 books. A helper can carry 4 boxes per trip and charges <m>\$6</m> per trip. data.problem: Claire's mom is trying to find a contractor to work on their house. The first contractor charges <m>\$53</m> per hour. The second contractor charges <m>\$69</m> per hour, but Claire's mom found a special deal online which will deduct <m>\$174</m> from the total bill. If her mom needs the chosen contractor to work for 12 hours, how will the potential bills compare? Which contractor is the better deal?
data.solution: To find the total cost for each contractor, we multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours needed. The total cost for the first contractor is <m>\$53</m> per hour multiplied by 12 hours, which equals <m>\$636</m>. The total cost for the second contractor is <m>\$69</m> per hour multiplied by 12 hours minus the <m>\$174</m> discount, which equals <m>\$654</m>. Therefore, the total bill will be <m>\$18</m> more if they choose the second contractor. Claire and her mom should hire the first contractor.

Summing up 1/4 ft + 4/5 ft + 1 ft gives us a total of 2 1/20 ft of twine needed overall. Brielle has enough twine to complete all three projects because she needs 2 1/20 ft and has 3 3/5 ft on hand.

data.problem: One fall night, the temperature rose 8 degrees between 12:00 AM and 4:00 AM. By 6:00 AM, the temperature fell 5 degrees from what it was at 4:00 AM. By 8:00 AM, it tripled from what it was at 6:00 AM. If the temperature was <m>3</m> degrees at 8:00 AM, what was the original temperature at 12:00 AM?
data.solution: The final temperature is given and the starting one is not, so work backwards, undoing each change in turn. At 8:00 AM it was <m>3</m> degrees. Between 6:00 AM and 8:00 AM the temperature tripled, so divide: <m>3 \div 3 = 1</m>, so at 6:00 AM it was <m>1</m> degrees. Between 4:00 AM and 6:00 AM the temperature fell 5 degrees, so add them back: <m>1 + 5 = 6</m>, so at 4:00 AM it was <m>6</m> degrees. Between 12:00 AM and 4:00 AM the temperature rose 8 degrees, so take those away: <m>6 - 8 = -2</m>. The original temperature was <m>-2</m> degrees.

data.problem: Emmett's mom is trying to find a contractor to work on their house. The first contractor charges <m>\$72</m> per hour. The second contractor charges <m>\$84</m> per hour, but Emmett's mom found a special deal online which will deduct <m>\$350</m> from the total bill. If his mom needs the chosen contractor to work for 22 hours, how will the potential bills compare? Which contractor is the better deal?
data.solution: To find the total cost for each contractor, we multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours needed. The total cost for the first contractor is <m>\$72</m> per hour multiplied by 22 hours, which equals <m>\$1584</m>. The total cost for the second contractor is <m>\$84</m> per hour multiplied by 22 hours minus the <m>\$350</m> discount, which equals <m>\$1498</m>. Therefore, the total bill will be <m>\$86</m> more if they choose the first contractor. Emmett and his mom should hire the second contractor.

Dividing the first day's distance of 558 miles by 9 hours gives us 62 mph. Now we can calculate the number of miles driven on the second day by multiplying 62 mph by 2 hours, yielding 124 miles. Finally, adding together both distances gives a total of 682 miles.

data.problem: One winter night, the temperature rose 4 degrees between 12:00 AM and 2:00 AM. By 7:00 AM, the temperature doubled from what it was at 2:00 AM. By 12:00 PM, it fell 8 degrees from what it was at 7:00 AM. If the temperature was <m>-2</m> degrees at 12:00 PM, what was the original temperature at 12:00 AM?
data.solution: The final temperature is given and the starting one is not, so work backwards, undoing each change in turn. At 12:00 PM it was <m>-2</m> degrees. Between 7:00 AM and 12:00 PM the temperature fell 8 degrees, so add them back: <m>-2 + 8 = 6</m>, so at 7:00 AM it was <m>6</m> degrees. Between 2:00 AM and 7:00 AM the temperature doubled, so divide: <m>6 \div 2 = 3</m>, so at 2:00 AM it was <m>3</m> degrees. Between 12:00 AM and 2:00 AM the temperature rose 4 degrees, so take those away: <m>3 - 4 = -1</m>. The original temperature was <m>-1</m> degrees.

data.problem: Miguel's mom is trying to find a contractor to work on their house. The first contractor charges <m>\$70</m> per hour. The second contractor charges <m>\$84</m> per hour, but Miguel's mom found a special deal online which will deduct <m>\$222</m> from the total bill. If his mom needs the chosen contractor to work for 12 hours, how will the potential bills compare? Which contractor is the better deal?
data.solution: To find the total cost for each contractor, we multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours needed. The total cost for the first contractor is <m>\$70</m> per hour multiplied by 12 hours, which equals <m>\$840</m>. The total cost for the second contractor is <m>\$84</m> per hour multiplied by 12 hours minus the <m>\$222</m> discount, which equals <m>\$786</m>. Therefore, the total bill will be <m>\$54</m> more if they choose the first contractor. Miguel and his mom should hire the second contractor.

data.ans_text_1: Nevaeh had 14 hammers. She gave 6 hammers to Abraham. How many hammers does Nevaeh have now?
data.ans_text_2: Harper has 8 more dimes than Jayla. Jayla has 15 dimes. How many dimes does Harper have?
data.ans_text_3: Adalynn has 17 craft materials. Of those craft materials, 3 are buttons and the rest are beads. How many beads does Adalynn have?
data.ans_text_4: Clara had some 9-volt batteries. She gave 3 to Ashton. Now Clara has 14 9-volt batteries left. How many 9-volt batteries did Clara have to begin with?

exercises.html:
For each of the following, write a word problem which is best suited for the given context. Your word problem should be appropriate for elementary school students, use sentences with proper English grammar, and require only one operation for solving. You should not solve your word problems.

  1. Separate - Result Unknown

    Nevaeh had 14 hammers. She gave 6 hammers to Abraham. How many hammers does Nevaeh have now?

    (This can be modeled by the equation \(14 - 6 = \Box\).)

  2. Compare - Larger Quantity Unknown

    Harper has 8 more dimes than Jayla. Jayla has 15 dimes. How many dimes does Harper have?

    (This can be modeled by the equation \(15 + 8 = \Box\).)

  3. Part-Part-Whole - One Part Unknown

    Adalynn has 17 craft materials. Of those craft materials, 3 are buttons and the rest are beads. How many beads does Adalynn have?

    (This can be modeled by the equation \(14 + \Box = 17\).)

  4. Separate - Start Unknown

    Clara had some 9-volt batteries. She gave 3 to Ashton. Now Clara has 14 9-volt batteries left. How many 9-volt batteries did Clara have to begin with?

    (This can be modeled by the equation \(\Box - 3 = 14\).)

data.answer: The number 413 is composite. We already know that 413 has two divisors: 1 and 413. outcomes.title: Greatest Common Divisor
outcomes.description: I can compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two numbers using appropriate methods.
outcomes.template:
Find {{listing_prob}} using the listing method (sometimes called the set intersection method). You must show correct lists and a final answer.

Divisors of {{listing_a}}: {{listing_list_a}}

Divisors of {{listing_b}}: {{listing_list_b}}

The largest divisor appearing in both lists simultaneously is {{listing_gcd}}, so {{listing_prob}} = {{listing_gcd}}

Find {{factorization_prob}} using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorization(s) before giving the final answer.

Prime factorization of {{factorization_a}}: {{factorization_mult_a}}

Prime factorization of {{factorization_b}}: {{factorization_mult_b}}

Multiplying together all common factors gives us {{factorization_mult_gcd}}, so {{factorization_prob}} = {{factorization_gcd}}

data.listing_prob_wording: using a method of your choice \textbf{other than} the prime factorization method. You must show your work before giving the final answer.

exercises.html:
1. Find \(\text{GCD}(76,92)\) using the listing method (sometimes called the set intersection method). You must show correct lists and a final answer.

    Divisors of \(76\): 1, 2, 4, 19, 38, 76

    Divisors of \(92\): 1, 2, 4, 23, 46, 92

    The largest divisor appearing in both lists simultaneously is 4, so \(\text{GCD}(76,92) = 4\)

  2. Find \(\text{GCD}(429,507)\) using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorization(s) before giving the final answer.

    Prime factorization of \(429\): \(3 \times 11 \times 13\)

    Prime factorization of \(507\): \(3 \times 13 \times 13\)

    Multiplying together all common factors gives us \(3 \times 13\), so \(\text{GCD}(429,507) = 39\)

    Divisors of \(32\): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32

    Divisors of \(64\): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64

    The largest divisor appearing in both lists simultaneously is 32, so \(\text{GCD}(32,64) = 32\)

  2. Find \(\text{GCD}(270,297)\) using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorization(s) before giving the final answer.

    Prime factorization of \(270\): \(2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5\)

    Prime factorization of \(297\): \(3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 11\)

    Multiplying together all common factors gives us \(3 \times 3 \times 3\), so \(\text{GCD}(270,297) = 27\)

(Some) multiples of 14: 14, 28, 42, 56, 70, 84, 98, 112, 126, 140, 154, 168, 182...

(Some) multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, 108, 120, 132, 144, 156, 168, 180...

The smallest nonzero multiple appearing in both lists simultaneously is 84, so \text{LCM}(14,12) = 84

Find \text{LCM}(180,390) using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorizations before giving the final answer. You may leave your answer in factored form.

Prime factorization of 180: 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5

Prime factorization of 390: 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 13

Multiplying together all prime factors of 180 and 390, then removing the overlapping prime factors gives us 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 13, so \text{LCM}(180,390) = 2340

1. Find \(\text{LCM}(70,30)\) using the listing method (sometimes called the set intersection method). You must show correct lists and a final answer.

    (Some) multiples of \(70\): 70, 140, 210, 280, 350, 420, 490...

    (Some) multiples of \(30\): 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240, 270, 300, 330, 360, 390, 420, 450...

    The smallest nonzero multiple appearing in both lists simultaneously is 210, so \(\text{LCM}(70,30) = 210\)

  2. Find \(\text{LCM}(182,546)\) using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorizations before giving the final answer. You may leave your answer in factored form.

    Prime factorization of \(182\): \(2 \times 7 \times 13\)

    Prime factorization of \(546\): \(2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 13\)

    Multiplying together all prime factors of \(182\) and \(546\), then removing the overlapping prime factors gives us \(2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 13\), so \(\text{LCM}(182,546) = 546\)

data.listing_prob_wording: using the listing method (sometimes called the set intersection method). You must show correct lists and a final answer.

exercises.html:
1. Find \(\text{LCM}(49,21)\) using the listing method (sometimes called the set intersection method). You must show correct lists and a final answer.

    (Some) multiples of \(49\): 49, 98, 147, 196, 245, 294, 343...

    (Some) multiples of \(21\): 21, 42, 63, 84, 105, 126, 147, 168, 189, 210, 231, 252, 273, 294, 315...

    The smallest nonzero multiple appearing in both lists simultaneously is 147, so \(\text{LCM}(49,21) = 147\)

  2. Find \(\text{LCM}(504,2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7)\) using the prime factorization method. You must show your factorizations before giving the final answer. You may leave your answer in factored form.

    Prime factorization of \(504\): \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 7\)

    Prime factorization of \(2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\): \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\)

    Multiplying together all prime factors of \(504\) and \(2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\), then removing the overlapping prime factors gives us \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\), so \(\text{LCM}(504,2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7) = 2520\)

outcomes.title: Explaining Fraction Models
outcomes.description: I can explain how to construct fraction models, and how students can understand how they represent the numerator and denominator of a fraction.
outcomes.template:
Suppose a student of yours is asked to complete the following fraction modeling task:

{{p1_text}}{{p1_math}}.

Construct the desired model. Then explain each step of its construction process. How is the denominator represented in the model? How is the numerator represented? How does each inform the construction process?

{{p1_soln_text}}

data.p1_text: If one regular hexagon represents 1, draw an area model for
data.p1_soln_text: The denominator of 2 tells us to split the whole (represented by a regular hexagon) into 2 equal parts. The numerator of  3 tells us to select 3 of the 2 parts. We show this selection by shading. Thus, we have a model of the fraction 3/2.
data.p1_ans_text: A model of regular hexagon(s) each split equally into 2 parts. A total of 3  of these parts are shaded to represent 3/2.

exercises.html:
1. Suppose a student of yours is asked to complete the following fraction modeling task:

    If one regular hexagon represents 1, draw an area model for \(\dfrac{3}{2}\).

    Construct the desired model. Then explain each step of its construction process. How is the denominator represented in the model? How is the numerator represented? How does each inform the construction process?

    The denominator of 2 tells us to split the whole (represented by a regular hexagon) into 2 equal parts. The numerator of 3 tells us to select 3 of the 2 parts. We show this selection by shading. Thus, we have a model of the fraction 3/2.

outcomes.title: Explaining the Denseness Property
outcomes.description: I can explain the denseness property of the rational numbers, by using language appropriate for an elementary student, and by using concrete examples.
outcomes.template:
In language appropriate for an elementary student, what does the denseness property of the rational numbers say?

Answers will vary.

Suppose a student challenged you to find {{expl_how_many}} numbers between {{num_a}} and {{num_b}}. What steps would you take to find those {{expl_how_many}} numbers? (You do not need to write out the actual {{expl_how_many}} individual numbers.)

Answers will vary.

data.problem: For every flag of Norfair, the ratio of its length to its width must be 13:6. If a Norfairian flag is to be produced with a length of 16 \frac{2}{3} ft, what should its width be? Give your final answer as a mixed number, if necessary.
data.solution: If we place the given ratio in a proportion with our known length and unknown width (being careful to attend to matching the order of length and width the numerators and denominators), we get <m mode="display"> \dfrac{13}{6} = \dfrac{16 \frac{2}{3}}{x}, </m> where <m>x</m> is the unknown width. Solving this proportion, we get <m mode="display"> x = 7 \frac{9}{13}.</m>

data.problem: Harmony and Henry just completed their contract work for the Faceplant company. Harmony worked a total of 22 hours, while Henry worked 33 hours. For their combined work, Faceplant sent them <m>\$1540</m>. If they decide that the fairest way to split the money in a way that reflects the amount of time each of them worked, how much money will each person receive?
data.solution: One way to solve this is by finding the hourly rate for their work. Since they made a total of <m>\$1540</m> over a collective 55 hours of work, we can divide to find that they were making <m>\$28</m> per hour. Now, we can multiply this unit rate by each person's hours worked. Doing so shows us that Harmony should receive <m>\$616</m>, and Henry should receive <m>\$924</m>.

data.problem: Austin and Gianna just completed their contract work for the LinkedOut company. Austin worked a total of 105 hours, while Gianna worked 26 hours. For their combined work, LinkedOut sent them <m>\$5109</m>. If they decide that the fairest way to split the money in a way that reflects the amount of time each of them worked, how much money will each person receive?
data.solution: One way to solve this is by finding the hourly rate for their work. Since they made a total of <m>\$5109</m> over a collective 131 hours of work, we can divide to find that they were making <m>\$39</m> per hour. Now, we can multiply this unit rate by each person's hours worked. Doing so shows us that Austin should receive <m>\$4095</m>, and Gianna should receive <m>\$1014</m>.

data.problem: Eliza and Kaiden just completed their contract work for the Mindendo company. Eliza worked a total of 49 hours, while Kaiden worked 19 hours. For their combined work, Mindendo sent them <m>\$1887</m>. If they decide that the fairest way to split the money in a way that reflects the amount of time each of them worked, how much money will each person receive?
data.solution: One way to solve this is by finding the hourly rate for their work. Since they made a total of <m>\$1887</m> over a collective 68 hours of work, we can divide to find that they were making <m>\$27.75</m> per hour. Now, we can multiply this unit rate by each person's hours worked. Doing so shows us that Eliza should receive <m>\$1359.75</m>, and Kaiden should receive <m>\$527.25</m>.

A farmers' market has 25 stalls. At one of them, 14 pounds of apples cost \$21. At the same price per pound, how many pounds of apples can you buy for \$15?

When attempting to solve the task, your student, Luna, wrote the following.

\frac{14}{25} \frac{14}{25} \times 15 = 8.4

Analyzing Luna's work, explain the following.

Describe the first step that Luna took to solve the problem. What model or strategy did Luna use? Which numbers from the problem did Luna work with first?

Luna started by dividing 14 by 25, which is the number of stalls, 25. As in a ratio model, she compared two numbers and used the comparison to multiply 15, but the two numbers she chose first do not describe the same moment in the problem.

Analyze Luna's work. Was the model or strategy used accurately? Did Luna get the correct answer? Explain how you made your decision about the accuracy.

No. 25 is not part of the relationship between the weight of apples and the cost; it is extra information. The ratio has to come from 14 and 21, which happen together: \frac{14}{21} = \frac{2}{3}, and \frac{2}{3} \times 15 = 10. Using a ratio was a good idea, but Luna put the wrong numbers in it, so the answer of 8.4 is incorrect. The correct answer is 10: you can buy 10 pounds of apples.

outcomes.title: Explaining Decimal Place Values with Blocks
outcomes.description: I can explain the relationship between place values in the base ten decimal system, and how the base ten blocks help demonstrate that relationship.
outcomes.template:
If one {{units_block}} represents one unit, which type of block represents one tenth? Why? Relate your answer back to the base ten place value system.

It takes ten tenths to create a single unit. Likewise, it takes ten {{tenths_block}}s to create a single {{units_block}}. Thus, a {{tenths_block}} represents one tenth.

If one {{units_block}} represents one unit, which type of block represents one hundredth? Why? Relate your answer back to the base ten place value system.

It takes one hundred hundredths to create a single unit. Likewise, it takes one hundred {{hundredths_block}}s to create a single {{units_block}}. Thus, a {{hundredths_block}} represents one hundredth.

How do base-ten blocks physically demonstrate how a base-ten place value system works?

In a base-ten place value system, each place value must be ten times the place value to its right. It takes ten units to make a long, ten longs to make a flat, and ten flats to make a large cube. Thus, the four types of base ten blocks can be used for any 4 consecutive base-ten place values.

data.problem: Harper checks her phone notifications. One of her notifications says that the value of Zamzung stock went up by <m>27.6\%</m>. If Harper originally owned <m>\$770.13</m> in Zamzung stock before this increase, how much is their investment worth now?
data.solution: First, we need to find how much more her stock is worth. Multiplying <m>\$770.13</m> by <m>0.276</m> shows us that her investment is worth <m>\$212.56</m> more. If we add this to the original value of <m>\$770.13</m>, we see that her investment is now worth <m>\$982.69</m>.
